body: Stepping from doing the work to leading the people who do it is a real shift. Over roughly the next ninety days, these short notes will keep you company as you grow into it.
For now, simply notice how much of your day still goes on the work you used to do. No blame, just an honest picture of where you are starting.
Nearly every new leader keeps reaching for their old tasks. Familiar work feels safe when everything else is new.
Think about the best manager you ever had. What did they do that made you want to give your best?
You were probably promoted for being good at the job. Leading asks for different skills, and it is fine not to have them all yet.
Watch for the moments you take over a task because it would be quicker to do it yourself. That instinct is worth recognising.
Feeling like an impostor is very common in a first leadership role. It usually means you care about doing it well.
Your old peers may now report to you. Allow some awkwardness on both sides while everyone adjusts.
Pay attention to how you measure a good day now. If it is still only about your own output, the old identity is in charge.
Consider what kind of leader you fear becoming. Naming it can help you steer gently away.
Leading can feel lonely at first. Fewer people to vent to and more decisions that are yours alone take getting used to.
Ask yourself how much you are talking in team meetings compared with listening. The balance may surprise you.
You may notice a pull to have every answer. Good leaders often say, "I'm not sure yet, let's work it out."
Look at how you react when someone does a task differently from how you would. Different is not always worse.
The urge to check every detail often comes from caring deeply about quality. It can still leave your team feeling untrusted.
Reflect on what you miss about your old role. Grieving it a little is part of moving on.
Some of the most important leadership work is invisible. Unblocking, encouraging and thinking ahead rarely show up on a to-do list.
Pay attention to whom you speak with most and whom you rarely check in with. Attention tends to drift to the loudest voices.
You might be tempted to be liked by everyone. Fairness and clarity tend to earn more respect in the long run.
When a decision feels heavy, notice where in your body you carry it. Stress shows up physically before we admit it.
Mistakes in this new role are part of learning it. Nobody begins leading people already knowing how.
Think about the expectations you have not yet said out loud. Teams struggle most with standards they have to guess.
Your calendar tells a story about your priorities. Look at this week's and see what it says.
Let go of any shame about how this role has felt so far. Growing into it is the whole point.
Being responsible for others can stir up anxiety. Remember that you do not have to carry every outcome alone.
Book a short one-to-one with each person on your team, if you have not already. Ask what helps them do their best work.
Pick one task you would normally do yourself and hand it over today, along with the context and a clear outcome.
In your next meeting, ask a question before you share your opinion. Let others shape the thinking first.
Write down the three outcomes your team most needs this month. Use them to decide what you say yes and no to.
Practise saying, "What do you think we should do?" when someone brings you a problem. Then genuinely weigh their answer.
Give one piece of specific, sincere praise today. "Your summary made that client call so much easier" beats a vague "great job".
Block out half an hour this week for thinking rather than doing. Leading needs time to look ahead.
When you delegate, agree when you will check in, and then resist checking sooner. Trust grows when you keep that promise.
If you have avoided a tricky conversation, plan the first sentence now. Starting is usually the hardest part.
Try ending meetings by asking, "What's unclear?" It catches confusion before it becomes rework.
Share the reasoning behind a decision, not just the decision itself. People commit more readily when they understand why.
When feedback is needed, keep it about the work and the impact, not the person. Clear and kind can go together.
Ask a team member what one thing you could do differently to support them. Listen without defending yourself.
Keep a simple note of each person's goals and interests. Remembering them shows that you see people, not just roles.
If you snapped at someone under pressure, go back and own it. A short apology builds more trust than pretending it never happened.
Protect your team from unnecessary noise this week. Not every request from above needs to land on their desks straight away.
Try a meeting where you speak last. You may hear ideas that would never have surfaced otherwise.
Give someone a stretch opportunity, with support close by. Growing others is one of the quiet joys of leading.
Some days you will slip back into doing everything yourself. Notice it, forgive it and hand something back tomorrow.
Ask your own manager what success in your role looks like to them. Clarity upwards makes leading downwards much easier.
When a project goes wrong, start with "What did we learn?" rather than "Whose fault was it?" Blame shuts people down.
Celebrate a small team win today, even briefly. Momentum is built on noticing progress.
Write down how you want your team to describe working with you. Let that guide one choice this week.
If you feel out of your depth, find another new leader to swap notes with. Shared uncertainty is surprisingly reassuring.
Try saying "I don't know" out loud in a meeting. Watch how it gives others permission to be honest too.
Before a big meeting, decide the one thing you most want people to leave knowing. Then say it plainly, near the start.
Ask each person on your team how they prefer to receive feedback. Some like it straight away, others want time to think.
Turn one of your recurring status meetings into a written update this week. Give everyone that hour back for real work.
If a team member seems flat or distant, check in privately and simply ask how they are doing. Then listen properly to the answer.
Look for a recurring task that could become someone else's to own. Ownership grows confidence far more than instructions do.
When someone disagrees with you, thank them for raising it. Teams that can push back tend to catch problems early.
Give yourself a proper lunch break today. Leaders who run on empty make shakier decisions.
Set one clear expectation that has been fuzzy. Say what good looks like, by when, and why it matters.
A difficult week does not mean you are bad at this. It means you are doing something genuinely hard.
Invite quieter team members into the conversation directly. "I'd love your take on this" can open a door.
Spend a few minutes after each one-to-one jotting down what you promised. Following through is where credibility lives.
If you catch yourself rewriting someone's work, pause. Could you coach them through the change instead?
Choose one decision you have been sitting on and make it today. A good decision now often beats a perfect one later.
Notice when you are tempted to rescue someone from a challenge. Sometimes support means letting them find their own way.
Share some context from above that your team rarely hears. Understanding the bigger picture helps people make better choices.
Try walking into a busy day with one question: what does my team need from me most today?
When you receive criticism, sit with it overnight before responding. Fresh eyes make it easier to take what is useful.
Thank someone for something they did weeks ago that you never acknowledged. It is never too late.
You are becoming someone who measures success by how well others are doing. That is a profound change of identity.
Look at what your team now handles without you. That freedom is something you built.
You no longer need to be the expert in every detail. Your value lies more and more in clarity, support and good judgement.
You are becoming a leader people can bring bad news to. That kind of safety is rare and precious.
Think about how differently you spend your days compared with when you started. The shift may be bigger than you realise.
Confidence in leading tends to arrive quietly, through decisions made and conversations survived. Yours is building.
You are becoming someone who makes space for others to shine. Their successes are now part of your story too.
Old habits like hoarding tasks may return on stressful days. You know them well now, and you can choose differently.
Your team is learning what to expect from you. Consistency, more than brilliance, is what helps them settle.
Remember that leadership is learned in practice, not handed over with a job title. You have been practising every day.
You are becoming someone who asks before telling. People grow more under that kind of leader.
Consider a moment when you held back and let someone else lead. What did it teach you about trust?
The person who first stepped into this role would be glad to see how you handle things now.
Your own wellbeing is part of good leadership. A steady leader helps create a steady team.
You are becoming someone who sees potential in others before they see it in themselves. That is a gift worth keeping.
Hard calls will still come, and some will still feel uncomfortable. That discomfort is a sign of care, not weakness.
Let yourself enjoy this role a little more. Leading people can be deeply rewarding when you stop trying to do it all.
Think about who might one day step into leadership because of how you supported them. That is a legacy in the making.
Look back over these months and pick the moment you felt most like a leader. What made it feel that way?
Which practice made the biggest difference, the one-to-ones, the delegating or the speaking last? Keep it at the centre of your week.
You will keep meeting new challenges as a leader. You now have a way of learning through them rather than freezing.
Take a moment to thank those who helped you grow into this role, including the team who were patient while you learned.
Leading others has asked you to grow as a person, not just as a professional. Be proud of that quieter growth.
This is the last note in this series. Keep leading with curiosity and care, and remember that the people you lead are the real measure of your work.
